Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time' in a severe childhood domestic-violence PTSD profile. Marked ease of verbal access is hard to reconcile with intensely distressing recall as a defining memory style, especially when the formulation emphasizes reciprocal Threat–Memory and Threat–Negative Appraisals links rather than a well-processed narrative memory. The pair could occasionally coexist, but here the contradiction is strong enough to question coherence of the selected memory items.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items describe opposing states during recall—detached/numb recall versus recall that consistently re-evokes the same terror. Both can occur across different moments in PTSD, but presented together as co-selected core memory descriptors without qualification they are internally tensioned and are the clearest coherence problem in the profile. The rest of the profile is broadly plausible for severe PTSD after witnessing childhood domestic violence, and the Threat/Negative Appraisals linkage fits the formulation.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a current expectation of direct interpersonal harm from others and a generalized startle/hypervigilance profile, whereas the trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood. That can be possible, but in this profile the danger focus is on strangers/other people harming the patient, which is not well anchored by the other nodes.

issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items focus on justice/accountability for perpetrators, but for childhood witnessed domestic violence this emphasis is somewhat hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on reliving terror and generalized threat. These appraisals do not connect well to the selected threat items or to the formulation's strong Threat↔Negative Appraisals linkage.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For childhood witnessed domestic violence, hypervigilance and bodily alarm are plausible, but specifically watching other people for signs that they might harm me implies a generalized interpersonal threat focused on the self. That is harder to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on recall terror and injustice about what was witnessed rather than a coherent belief that others are currently likely to attack him.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: The appraisal that the responsible people faced no consequences is plausible in this trauma type, but paired with 'nothing has been done about it' it suggests an ongoing justice-focused grievance. This sits awkwardly with the threat and memory items, which emphasize re-experiencing terror rather than a clinically coherent meaning pattern linking current threat to the childhood domestic violence exposure.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: 'What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it' is somewhat mismatched to witnessed domestic violence in childhood because the trauma type is witnessing violence between others rather than a direct assault on the patient. While survivors can absolutely personalize the injustice, the phrasing 'happened to me' combined with the justice-focused theme is less coherent with the rest of the selected items than appraisals about safety, powerlessness, or lasting damage would be.

vignette: Ravi, a 36-year-old South Asian man and an accountant by profession, has been haunted by memories of the domestic violence he witnessed in his childhood. The traumatic event was deeply etched into his mind, and now Ravi finds himself constantly on guard, always ready to react to perceived threats. The vivid recollections of that night when he saw his father assault his mother continue to surface unexpectedly. These intrusive memories bring back the same intense feelings of terror he experienced as a child. The mere sound of raised voices or a sudden movement can instantly transport Ravi back to that moment, making him feel as though the violence is happening all over again. He struggles to articulate these experiences, often unable to put them into words, leaving him feeling isolated and misunderstood. Ravi's constant state of hypervigilance has become his primary way of coping with the ongoing sense of danger he perceives in everyday situations. His body feels perpetually tense, ready to spring into action at any sign of threat. This heightened alertness is exacerbated by his belief that nothing can be done to prevent bad things from happening again. The lack of accountability for those who were responsible for the violence has reinforced this feeling of helplessness. Ravi's negative appraisals play a significant role in maintaining his state of hypervigilance and intrusive memories. He feels certain that he cannot protect himself or others from further harm, which fuels his constant fear and tension. The belief that those who perpetrated the violence faced no consequences has left him feeling deeply frustrated and vulnerable. The memory of the violent event is particularly potent in Ravi's life because it aligns with his current negative beliefs about helplessness and lack of accountability. Every time a trigger occurs, whether at home or while performing his accounting duties, he finds himself reliving those traumatic moments. His belief that bad things will inevitably happen again makes him hyperaware of any potential dangers around him. Ravi's occupation as an accountant provides a backdrop against which these triggers are often encountered. The stress and pressure of his work, coupled with the sudden reminders of violence in his past, have made it increasingly difficult for him to focus on his tasks. He finds himself distracted by intrusive thoughts about the event and feels constantly tense at work. The cycle of negative beliefs, hypervigilance, and intrusive memories has become self-reinforcing over time. Ravi's belief that he cannot prevent bad things from happening leads to increased physical reactivity and hypervigilance, which in turn make it more likely for him to experience triggered memories. These experiences further solidify his negative appraisals, creating a relentless loop of fear and distress. What finally brought Ravi to seek help was the growing realization that his life had become unmanageable due to these symptoms. He is most afraid of being trapped in this cycle of terror and hopelessness indefinitely but also holds out hope for finding ways to regain control over his thoughts and reactions. Ravi hopes to learn how to navigate through his memories without feeling overwhelmed by fear, so he can reclaim a sense of happiness and peace in his daily life.
